pages.title: Welcome
pages.subtitle: The meeting is not the work

blocks.heading: What this planner is for
paragraphs: Most meeting templates end when the meeting ends. This one is built around what happens afterwards: who owes what, by when, and whether it arrived. The agenda pages exist to feed the trackers, not the other way round.

blocks.heading: The three things it holds
items: A cadence — the daily, weekly and monthly rhythm of meetings you actually hold
Ownership — every action attached to one name, and a responsibility chart when more than one person is involved
Follow-through — deadlines, chases, and a weekly review that asks whether last week's actions closed

blocks.heading: How to use it honestly
paragraphs: The Action Items Tracker and the Deadline Tracker are the only pages that matter after the first fortnight. If those two are current, the planner is working. If they are blank while the notes pages are full, you are recording meetings rather than running them.

blocks.heading: One rule worth keeping
paragraphs: An action with no owner and no date is not an action. It is a topic that came up. Write it in the notes and leave the tracker alone.

pages.title: Instructions
pages.subtitle: Set up in twenty minutes

blocks.heading: Choose your size
paragraphs: Four sizes are included and all four contain identical pages. A4 and US Letter suit the desk and the meeting room. A5 and Half Letter suit a tablet carried between rooms, and print two-up on a full sheet.

blocks.heading: Set up once
items: Read the Meeting Planning Guide
Fill the Annual Meeting Overview with the dates already fixed
List your standing meetings on a Monthly Meeting Planner page
Open one Action Items Tracker page and keep it open from now on

blocks.heading: Every meeting
items: Write the objective on a Meeting Objectives page before sending the invitation
Run the agenda page, capturing actions as they are agreed
Move every action to the Action Items Tracker before you leave the room
Put any date-bound item on the Deadline Tracker as well

blocks.heading: Digital use
items: Import the PDF as a document, not as an image
Switch to read mode to tap links, write mode to write
Use the Actions and Deadlines tabs to reach the trackers from any page

pages.title: Meeting Planning Guide
pages.subtitle: Six rules that shorten meetings

blocks.heading: Every meeting needs a decision or it needs cancelling
paragraphs: If you cannot write the decision the meeting must produce, the meeting is a status update and belongs in writing. The Meeting Objectives page exists to force that sentence before the invitation goes out.

blocks.heading: Invite the people who decide, copy the people who care
paragraphs: Six attendees is a meeting. Twelve is an audience. Everyone else receives the notes.

blocks.heading: Actions are assigned in the room, not afterwards
items: One owner per action — shared ownership is no ownership
A date, not "soon"
Read the actions aloud before closing
Anything with a hard date goes on the Deadline Tracker too

blocks.heading: Use the responsibility chart when more than two people are involved
paragraphs: Responsible, accountable, consulted, informed. Most missed deliverables are two people each believing the other was responsible. The chart costs five minutes and settles it.

blocks.heading: Chase before the deadline, not after
paragraphs: The Follow-up Planner has a Chase On column that sits ahead of the due date. Chasing afterwards is not follow-up, it is accounting for a failure.

blocks.heading: Review the meetings themselves once a week
paragraphs: The Weekly Review asks how many actions closed, not how many meetings were held. A calendar full of meetings and a tracker full of open items is the pattern this planner is designed to expose.
